title: Metadata polling & noise honeypot — personal lab notes
body:
Context / why I’m scribbling this down:

Quick problem statement: our labeling queues have a growing fraction of examples where the signal is effectively in the wrong place — yesterday’s tokenized text is fine but the surrounding metadata fields (session IDs, tracking params, legacy export blobs) are polluting model inputs and yielding spurious labels. Those rows are noisy, appear repeatedly, and bias heuristics (e.g., 'contains-url' or 'has-email') and downstream QA checks. We need a lightweight, deployable set of heuristics and a small ‘honeypot’ sampling strategy to detect and measure this class of noise, then surgical remediation steps that don’t trash good longtail examples.

Notes / heuristics brainstorm (rough order: detect -> quantify -> block/clean -> surface to human):

1) Detection signals (fast, cheap):
- high-metadata-ratio: ratio of non-text fields length to main_text length > 0.15 (tunable). Many noisy exports have a big JSON blob in a metadata column.
- repeated-pattern-id: metadata contains GUID-like token repeated across many rows in a short window (same import run).
- tracking-params: regex detect utm_|gclid|fbclid|session_id|referrer param substrings.
- header-bleed: fields named user_agent, x_forwarded_for, remote_addr -> likely not useful for labeling tasks.
- binary-blob-flag: base64-looking strings (>80% alnum+/=) or long hex strings in metadata.
- near-duplicate text with different meta: if same main_text appears N times with wildly different metadata, flag as ingestion duplication.

2) Honeypot / sampling plan (how to measure prevalence):
- daily small sample (n=2k rows) stratified by source and by newly ingested run id.
- annotate sample with 3 quick labels: "clean", "meta-dominant-noise", "duplication/ingest-batch". Keep the annotation fast (10s per row).
- gate: if meta-dominant > 6% of sample for a given source, trigger deeper pipeline: run remediation on that source and alert owner.

3) Lightweight remediation (automated safe defaults):
- strip-mostly-metadata: if high-metadata-ratio and main_text length < 240 chars, drop metadata fields from model input and add a tag in db: meta_stripped=true.
- normalize-utm: remove utm_*/gclid/fbclid substrings from URLs; collapse query strings to canonical form.
- collapse-duplicate-rows: de-dupe exact main_text duplicates within same import run (keep earliest), append import provenance to kept row.
- binary-blob-safelist: if field contains long base64 / hex, move to archival blob table and replace with placeholder 'archived_metadata_blob_v#'.
- manual-queue: anything that looks like potential PII (email-ish in meta, ssn-ish patterns) goes to small human review queue instead of auto-remediate.

4) Labeler-facing affordances (don’t remove context blindly):
- show stripped metadata on demand in UI (expandable) with reason for strip. Labeler can re-enable when needed.
- add a short reason tag for every auto-action ("stripped:utm", "de-duped", "archived-blob") so downstream audits can reconstruct what happened.

5) Metrics to track (make the fix measurable):
- % of rows flagged by detection heuristics per source per day.
- % of rows auto-remediated and how many re-enabled by labelers.
- labeler correction rate (labels that change after metadata un-hide). Large number means we were overzealous.
- time-to-surface: time between ingestion and honeypot flagging; aim <24h.

6) Quick regex / snippet library (proof-of-concept):
- utm regex: (?i)utm_[a-z]+=
- guid-ish: \b[0-9a-f]{8}(-[0-9a-f]{4}){3}-[0-9a-f]{12}\b
- base64-ish: ^[A-Za-z0-9\+/=]{200,}$ (heuristic for binary stored as text)
- email-in-meta: [A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}

7) Small test plan for a pilot (2 week window):
- Week 0: add detection flags and daily honeypot sampling (no auto-remediation). Measure baseline.
- Week 1: enable non-destructive remediation (strip in a shadow field, do not remove from original). Monitor labeler re-enable rate and false positives.
- Week 2: enable policy-driven auto-remediation for sources with low false-positive rates; send alerts for others.

Risks / unknowns / questions to follow up:
- We may have edge cases where metadata actually contains label-relevant info (e.g., app logs where the error code in meta is crucial). Need per-source whitelist config.
- How to handle downstream customers expecting original metadata? Store a reversible archival mapping.
- Interaction with privacy/PII pipelines: do we need to route suspected PII through redaction flow instead of human queue? Check legal.

Open todo (short):
- [ ] Build a small query job to find top 20 sources by meta-flag incidence (SQL w/ sample size 10k).
- [ ] Wire up daily honeypot sampler and simple annotation UI for the 3 quick labels.
- [ ] Draft a short contrib doc for data ingestion owners explaining default strip rules + whitelist path.
- [ ] Add a telemetry tag when labeler re-enables stripped metadata so we can compute correction rate.
- [ ] Confirm with privacy/legal about archiving vs deletion of binary metadata blobs.

Mini mental model notes (for myself):
- Two failure modes: (a) metadata noise that shouldn't affect labels but pollutes heuristics and duplicates; (b) metadata contains the signal. The logic needs to be conservative: prefer shadow/flagging first, auto-remediate only when source is stable and labeler feedback is low.

Small examples from prod (anonymized):
- row A: main_text='How do I reset my password?' meta has a 9k char JSON called 'raw_export' -> flagged as high-metadata-ratio.
- row B: main_text duplicated 17x across same import run; origin header shows same run_id -> de-dupe candidate.
- row C: main_text short chat excerpt but meta.user_agent contains an email address used by customer support -> escalate to manual review (possible signal).

If I had 20 minutes tomorrow I would:
- run the quick SQL to emit top 50 most frequent meta-key names and their avg value length (this usually surfaces the obvious culprits), and then sketch the WHITELIST/BLACKLIST per source mapping.

End notes: keep everything reversible during pilot. The aim is not to 'throw away' provenance — it's to reduce noise that drives labeler confusion and model misclassification while keeping traceability.
